items.title: Hackers Are Turning Claude, ChatGPT and Copilot Into Bait for Real Malware
items.summary: Cybercriminals are increasingly using trusted artificial intelligence names as a shortcut to infect users with malware. Fake download pages, browser extensions, search ads and shared AI conversations are being used to make harmful files and commands look legitimate. The campaigns target people looking for popular AI tools, coding assistants and productivity features. A victim may search for an installer, click a sponsored result, or install an apparently useful extension, only to receive a backdoor, password-stealing malware or a browser hijacker instead. Sophos researchers identified the trend after reviewing a year of managed detection and response investigations. Of 38 confirmed cases involving hostile AI activity, 30 involved software impersonation, showing that criminals are mainly abusing AI brands rather than using AI itself to run attacks. The impact reaches both individuals and organizations. Stolen browser sessions, saved passwords, private files and cryptocurrency wallet data can give attackers a foothold into wider business systems. Sophos said in a report shared with Cyber Security News (CSN) that the campaigns also exploit a difficult reality: users are more likely to trust an installation prompt when it carries a familiar AI name. Claude, ChatGPT and Copilot Into Bait for Real Malware Claude was the most frequently abused lure in Sophos’ review, appearing in 26 cases. Attackers used fake Claude, ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot pages to distribute malware through malicious ads, poisoned search results and domains designed to resemble legitimate vendor websites. Many incidents relied on InstallFix, a variation of the ClickFix social-engineering method. Instead of presenting a fake error page, the attacker offers a polished installation guide that tells visitors to copy and run a command. That command then downloads or launches the real payload. Fake Claude ‘InstallFix’ site (Source – Sophos) In one case, a fake Claude site directed victims to execute an mshta command that retrieved a Windows application package named claude or claude.msixbundle . A second command ran code directly in memory and attempted to hide its activity inside a browser process. This same approach has become a familiar entry point in wider malware operations. A recent ClickFix malware delivery campaign similarly used fake verification pages to convince Windows users to execute commands themselves, turning normal user actions into the start of an infection. Sophos also observed LummaStealer delivered through AI-branded infrastructure, as well as a fake Claude Setup.zip archive that planted a harmful libcef.dll file. Another repackaged claude.exe acted as a loader, while a more developed fake site used DLL sideloading to install the previously undocumented Beagle backdoor. The strongest early defense is still simple: obtain AI tools only from confirmed vendor domains. That advice matters because fake pages can closely copy official branding, layouts and download flows. Extensions and Trusted Platforms Abused The abuse does not stop at installers. Researchers found AI-themed browser extensions that presented themselves as useful assistants while collecting browser data and communicating with attacker-controlled servers. Since extensions can be granted broad access to sessions and stored credentials, they are especially attractive to data thieves. In one investigation, four customers installed a fake Perplexity extension that hijacked searches and sent browsing telemetry in real time. The extension redirected searches through perplexity-ai[.]online and displayed a landing page after installation, creating the appearance of a normal AI service. Uncensored Qwen3.5 build promoted in The Gentlemen ransomware group’s leaked internal chats (Source – Sophos) The danger is not limited to obscure download sites. Sophos found that one fake extension appeared in the Chrome Web Store with a 4.7-star rating, 67 reviews and 10,000 installs. That apparent credibility can reduce suspicion, much like the malicious AI extensions targeting enterprises that harvested conversations and browsing data. Attackers have also begun placing their lures on trusted services. In several macOS campaigns, the trick moved from fake brand pages to shared conversations hosted on legitimate ChatGPT infrastructure. Victims were then instructed to paste Terminal commands, a technique also seen in abused Claude shared chats used to spread information-stealing malware. Organizations should audit AI-related browser extensions, verify the publisher before installation and remove extensions that are not necessary. Security teams should also monitor for unusual command execution, suspicious PowerShell activity and browser processes launching system utilities, because the behavior remains detectable even when the initial lure uses a trusted AI brand. AI dependencies deserve the same supply-chain controls as other software packages. Sophos documented poisoned packages and malicious plugins that fetched remote code, warning that automated development tools could shrink the time between a malicious package being published and executed. items.title: CyberPanel Pre-Auth RCE Chain Lets Attackers Gain Server Shell via AI Scanner Flaws
items.summary: Security researchers have disclosed a critical pre-authentication RCE chain in CyberPanel that could let attackers gain a shell on vulnerable hosting servers without valid credentials. The attack combines weaknesses in the platform’s AI Scanner functionality with stored cross-site scripting and abuse of cron jobs. The issue affects CyberPanel versions earlier than 2.4.4. CyberPanel is a web hosting control panel for managing websites, DNS, email, databases, and server services. Because it serves as a central control plane, a successful compromise can grant attackers broad access to hosted environments. Pentera researchers identified the chain during an analysis of internet-facing hosting panels. The researchers found that CyberPanel contained an unauthenticated AI Scanner endpoint intended to receive scan data from an external service. CyberPanel Pre-Auth RCE Enables Server Shell The endpoint accepted user-controlled scan results and stored them in the application database without properly sanitizing the content. This created a stored cross-site scripting vulnerability tracked as CVE-2026-41472. An attacker could place malicious JavaScript in a forged scan result, but initially faced an important limitation: the request required a valid scan_id. Without a legitimate scan identifier, the application rejected the submitted result. cronCommand is explicitly excluded from security filtering due to its special characters ( source: Pentera ) The missing piece was an exposed debug API endpoint , /api/ai-scanner/list-api-keys. The endpoint could be accessed without authentication and returned information about recent AI scans, including valid scan IDs.. This access-control issue, tracked as CVE-2026-41473, allowed attackers to obtain the identifier needed to submit a malicious scan result. After obtaining a valid scan ID, an attacker could inject JavaScript into the stored scan record. The malicious code would not execute immediately. Instead, it would wait until a CyberPanel administrator opened the AI Scanner results page. When the administrator viewed the poisoned result, the script would run in the administrator’s authenticated browser session . The RCE chain (Source: Pentera) The attack code could then use the administrator’s active session and CSRF token to perform actions on the administrator’s behalf. Pentera researchers demonstrated that the script could silently create a new administrative account. This gave the attacker valid access to the CyberPanel dashboard without needing to steal a password directly. The final stage involved CyberPanel’s cron job management feature. After logging in with the newly created account, the attacker could create a website and associated system user, then abuse cron job functionality to execute a command on the server. Researchers found that the cronCommand parameter could dangerously allow shell command execution. This enabled the attacker to obtain a server shell. Nuclei template to check access to sensitive APIs (Source: Pentera) The chain demonstrates how several individually limited weaknesses can combine to become a full server takeover. The exposed API endpoint leaked data, stored XSS-enabled privilege abuse , and cron job handling enabled command execution. Pentera reported the vulnerabilities to CyberPanel on May 4, 2026. The CyberPanel team reportedly issued fixes within about four hours, including removal of debug endpoints, authentication for callback functionality, and output escaping. Administrators should update CyberPanel to the latest patched release immediately. Organizations unable to patch should turn off the AI Scanner feature and restrict access to /api/ai-scanner/list-api-keys and /api/ai-scanner/test-auth until updates can be deployed. Prevent incidents due to slow investigations. items.title: Police Are Hiding Their Use of Flock Surveillance Cameras
items.summary: A usage policy for Flock license plate reader cameras tells police not to talk about the cameras: When cops use Flock to arrest someone in Wapello County, Iowa, they don’t want them to know. A usage policy for the automated license plate reader cameras in the county tells police, in no uncertain terms, to keep them a secret: “DO NOT MENTION ALPR USAGE TO THE OCCUPANTS OF THE VEHICLE,” the policy document reads. “DO NOT MENTION ALPR USAGE IN YOUR REPORT OR COMPLAINT UNLESS ABSOLUTELY NECESSARY.” This reminds me of IMSI-catchers (Stingray was the most popular) a couple of decades ago. Police would go to even more extremes to hide their usage.

items.title: New “Zombie Card” Flaw Lets Expired Visa Cards Make Contactless Payments
items.summary: Security researchers have demonstrated that an expired credit card is not as dead as most cardholders believe. A new study from the University of Massachusetts Amherst, presented at the 35th USENIX Security Symposium, reveals a practical NFC relay attack dubbed “Zombie Card” that revives expired Visa contactless cards, allowing them to complete real purchases at point-of-sale terminals across multiple US banks. The core discovery is deceptively simple: card expiration in EMV contactless payments is enforced as a transaction policy check performed by the terminal, not as a cryptographic fact baked into the card itself. EMV contactless payment The private keys stored on a chip never expire, and the certificates that authenticate a card during Offline Data Authentication often remain valid well past the card’s printed date to smooth over reissuance periods. That leaves the actual expiry decision resting on a single data field, the Application Expiration Date, which the terminal reads in plaintext and checks locally. Zombie Card Back Online Researchers Raja Hasnain Anwar, Gerard DeCunha, and Muhammad Taqi Raza built a man-in-the-middle relay using two NFC-capable Android phones , one emulating the card near the POS terminal and one emulating the terminal near the physical card, communicating over Wi-Fi. NFC relay This setup lets them intercept and rewrite APDU data exchanged during the transaction’s data-retrieval phase in real time, using nothing more than commodity smartphones. Testing spanned EMV Kernel 2 (Mastercard), Kernel 4 (American Express), Kernel 6 (Discover), and Kernel 3 (Visa). Kernels 2, 4, and 6 detected tampering because expiry-related data is cryptographically bound to signed records or hashed transaction data, so any in-flight edit broke signature verification and killed the transaction. Kernel 3 was the outlier. Experimental setup Its expiration field is excluded from the signed dynamic application data, so flipping a past date to a future one slips past the terminal’s local check without breaking any signature. Making matters worse, Kernel 3 forwards an all-zero Terminal Verification Results field to the issuer, meaning banks never learn that the terminal’s local validation was manipulated. Combined with card-side flags that can force a transaction “online” even when expiry checks fail, this created an open path for an expired card carrying a still-valid Primary Account Number to reach the issuer’s authorization system unchallenged. The team validated the attack in a lab using SumUp terminals and then in the wild at retail and grocery merchants, across five major US banks, using their own expired and replaced cards to avoid any third-party harm. Results diverged by issuer: one bank approved zombie transactions across amounts up to $500 because it validated only the account and cryptogram rather than the specific card instance, while another consistently declined and prompted use of the replacement card. Notably, even a non-expired card that had already been replaced by its issuer continued processing successful payments on the same account. The researchers proposed countermeasures spanning every layer of the payment chain: cryptographically binding expiry data to signed records, forcing consistency checks between the terminal’s expiry field and the value sent to issuers, treating expiration and replacement as explicit issuer-side authorization predicates, and preserving genuine validation results instead of zeroing them out. They disclosed the findings to Visa and affected banks in May 2025, with Visa’s red team still reproducing the attack as of the paper’s acceptance, and no confirmed fixes deployed yet. Until systemic changes land, cardholders should follow standard advice: destroy expired cards by cutting through the chip and magnetic stripe rather than discarding them intact. items.title: 15 Malicious Firefox Extensions Abuse Cloudflare Workers to Exfiltrate Crypto Wallet Secrets
items.summary: Firefox users are facing a coordinated campaign of malicious add-ons that masquerade as cryptocurrency wallets, themes, and simple browser tools. The extensions can trick victims into disclosing recovery phrases, private keys, login details, and clipboard data, placing digital assets and online accounts at immediate risk. Active since at least March 2026, the operation spans 77 Firefox extension identities: 40 confirmed malicious add-ons and 37 deceptive sports-score shells that helped the group blend into the marketplace. Researchers at Socket.dev identified the campaign and provisionally call it Offside Wallet Theft Factory. It also gives operators a cheap way to rotate brands, infrastructure, and deceptive listings. Socket.dev said in a report shared with Cyber Security News (CSN) that reused code, shared infrastructure, deceptive descriptions, and changes to older extension identities point to a repeatable publishing operation. Representative attack flow for the confirmed malicious extensions (Source – Socket.dev) The findings show why an add-on’s stated purpose or modest permission request cannot establish trust. Samples used a notepad or sports application as cover while theft happened inside the extension or on a remote page. 15 Malicious Firefox Extensions Abuse Cloudflare Workers Fifteen of the malicious extensions embedded fake wallet screens or altered wallet code directly in their signed packages. They captured recovery phrases and private keys during wallet creation or import, then sent the data to attacker-controlled Cloudflare Workers deployments. This echoes Cloudflare Workers abuse cases , where a legitimate cloud service is misused to conceal hostile delivery or collection infrastructure. Several variants copied or modified Rabby-derived wallet code but used unrelated, theme-style names. Their implant intercepted new or imported 12-word and 24-word recovery phrases. Other samples presented counterfeit Portal, OKX, or generic Web3 import pages, relying on victims to type their secret rather than searching the browser for it. A recovery phrase can restore a wallet on another device, so an attacker who receives it can take control independently. Deleting the extension may stop additional collection, but it cannot make a disclosed phrase safe again. The 0KX WEB3 listing was live during our analysis and presented the extension as a cryptocurrency wallet (Source – Socket.dev) The risk follows the wallet stealing add-on problem: trust in an apparently useful browser tool becomes the path to account takeover. A separate group of 13 modified Rabby-style extensions took a quieter route. Before the wallet software encrypted and saved its keyring data locally, altered code sent the serialized keyrings to hardcoded HTTP servers. Because the data left first, normal local encryption offered no protection for the copied information. Repurposed Add-Ons Expand the Campaign Seven extensions used a remote-control design built around attacker-managed Supabase projects. One example, 0KX WEB3, advertised wallet features but contained no real wallet functions. Instead, it loaded a remote website in its popup, displayed a decoy notepad when inactive, and opened the supplied page after installation or an update. The remote page asked users to create or import a wallet and then requested a recovery phrase or private key. This staged approach makes review harder because operators can switch an extension between harmless-looking and phishing content without republishing it. items.summary_html:
Firefox users are facing a coordinated campaign of malicious add-ons that masquerade as cryptocurrency wallets, themes, and simple browser tools.

The extensions can trick victims into disclosing recovery phrases, private keys, login details, and clipboard data, placing digital assets and online accounts at immediate risk.

Active since at least March 2026, the operation spans 77 Firefox extension identities: 40 confirmed malicious add-ons and 37 deceptive sports-score shells that helped the group blend into the marketplace.

Researchers at Socket.dev identified the campaign and provisionally call it Offside Wallet Theft Factory. It also gives operators a cheap way to rotate brands, infrastructure, and deceptive listings.

Socket.dev said in a report shared with Cyber Security News (CSN) that reused code, shared infrastructure, deceptive descriptions, and changes to older extension identities point to a repeatable publishing operation.

Representative attack flow for the confirmed malicious extensions (Source – Socket.dev)

The findings show why an add-on’s stated purpose or modest permission request cannot establish trust. Samples used a notepad or sports application as cover while theft happened inside the extension or on a remote page.

15 Malicious Firefox Extensions Abuse Cloudflare Workers

Fifteen of the malicious extensions embedded fake wallet screens or altered wallet code directly in their signed packages.

They captured recovery phrases and private keys during wallet creation or import, then sent the data to attacker-controlled Cloudflare Workers deployments.

This echoes Cloudflare Workers abuse cases, where a legitimate cloud service is misused to conceal hostile delivery or collection infrastructure.

Several variants copied or modified Rabby-derived wallet code but used unrelated, theme-style names. Their implant intercepted new or imported 12-word and 24-word recovery phrases.

Other samples presented counterfeit Portal, OKX, or generic Web3 import pages, relying on victims to type their secret rather than searching the browser for it.

A recovery phrase can restore a wallet on another device, so an attacker who receives it can take control independently. Deleting the extension may stop additional collection, but it cannot make a disclosed phrase safe again.

The 0KX WEB3 listing was live during our analysis and presented the extension as a cryptocurrency wallet (Source – Socket.dev)

The risk follows the wallet stealing add-on problem: trust in an apparently useful browser tool becomes the path to account takeover. A separate group of 13 modified Rabby-style extensions took a quieter route.

Before the wallet software encrypted and saved its keyring data locally, altered code sent the serialized keyrings to hardcoded HTTP servers. Because the data left first, normal local encryption offered no protection for the copied information.

Repurposed Add-Ons Expand the Campaign

Seven extensions used a remote-control design built around attacker-managed Supabase projects. One example, 0KX WEB3, advertised wallet features but contained no real wallet functions.

Instead, it loaded a remote website in its popup, displayed a decoy notepad when inactive, and opened the supplied page after installation or an update.

The remote page asked users to create or import a wallet and then requested a recovery phrase or private key. This staged approach makes review harder because operators can switch an extension between harmless-looking and phishing content without republishing it.

It also reinforces lessons from recent extension supply chain attacks, where a later update can change a trusted tool into a data-stealing one. Five more extensions collected credentials and clipboard contents through a hardcoded command-and-control server.

Clipboard theft can expose copied passwords, authentication material, wallet addresses, or private keys.

Investigators also found 37 add-ons that claimed to provide unrelated utilities but were actually repackaged sports-score applications; nine malicious identities had older sports-score versions before turning into wallet stealers.

Users and security teams should remove listed extensions, review add-ons again after every update, and verify publishers through official project channels before installing wallet software.

Do not enter a recovery phrase or private key into a browser popup or webpage. Anyone who entered either secret into a suspect extension should treat it as permanently compromised, move assets to a newly created wallet, and replace exposed credentials.

This is especially important given earlier malicious Firefox extension activity, which showed that add-ons can also target passwords and OAuth tokens.

items.title: Splunk Patches Critical MCP Server RCE and 16 Other Security Flaws Across AI Toolkit, Kafka Apps
items.summary: Splunk has released security updates for 17 vulnerabilities affecting several apps and add-ons, including Splunk MCP Server, Splunk AI Toolkit, and Splunk Connect for Kafka. The most severe issue, tracked as CVE-2026-76404, is a critical remote code execution vulnerability with a CVSS score of 9.1.  The advisory, published on August 19, 2026, also covers Cisco Talos Intelligence for Enterprise Security Cloud and Splunk On-Call (VictorOps). Organizations using the affected components should prioritize upgrades, especially where administrative interfaces, REST APIs, or AI model-management features are exposed to untrusted users or networks. Splunk Patches Security Flaws CVE-2026-76404 affects Splunk MCP Server app versions earlier than 1.2.1. Splunk said an authenticated user with the admin role could execute arbitrary commands on the underlying operating system. The flaw exists in the app’s credential-management component. Missing input validation allows unsafe deserialization of stored data without confirming that the supplied content has the expected type. This creates a path for malicious serialized objects to execute commands. The vulnerability is categorized as CWE-502, or deserialization of untrusted data . Administrators should upgrade the Splunk MCP Server app to version 1.2.1. Until patching is complete, Splunk recommends disabling or removing the app. Splunk AI Toolkit received fixes for nine vulnerabilities, including several high-severity access-control and code-execution flaws. The most serious, CVE-2026-76395, carries a CVSS score of 8.8 and could allow a user with the power role to run arbitrary code on a Splunk server by loading a crafted model containing malicious sparse matrix data. The issue stems from unsafe deserialization of embedded pickle content. Other AI Toolkit flaws could allow lower-privileged users to perform searches with system-level privileges, manage containers and connections without proper authorization , access or delete other users’ experiment history, and modify scheduled searches that run under the search owner’s permissions. Splunk AI Toolkit versions below 6.0.0 are affected by most of these issues, while two flaws affect versions below 6.0.1. Users on the 5.7 release line should upgrade to version 6.0.0, while users already on version 6.0 should move to 6.0.1. These include an SSRF flaw, CVE-2026-76402, rated 8.2, which could allow an unauthenticated attacker with access to the Kafka Connect REST API to configure a non-secure HTTP Event Collector endpoint and capture connector authentication credentials. The Kafka fixes also address two denial-of-service issues and improper certificate validation in Kerberos-authenticated HTTP Event Collector deployments. Splunk advises restricting Kafka Connect REST API access to trusted administrative systems and networks, enforcing secure transport for HTTP Event Collector endpoints, and applying finite retry limits. Additional fixes include an SSRF vulnerability in Cisco Talos Intelligence for Enterprise Security Cloud and partial API key disclosure in Splunk On-Call (VictorOps). Updated versions are 1.0.3 for the Talos app and 1.0.43 for Splunk On-Call. Organizations should inventory installed Splunk apps, apply relevant updates, restrict access to the management API, and review administrative and power-role assignments for signs of unnecessary privilege exposure. items.title: Claude AI Finds SAML Security Flaws That Can Let Attackers Take Over Accounts
items.summary: Security researchers have used Anthropic’s Claude AI to uncover serious flaws in Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) implementations that could allow attackers to bypass authentication and take over user accounts. The findings highlight the persistent security risks created by XML signature processing, inconsistent parser behavior, and custom SAML code. A researcher at Oblique Security built an AI-assisted testing harness around Claude Opus to examine SAML libraries and applications. Rather than directing the model to reproduce known bugs, the system supplied a threat model and let Claude explore how each implementation handled signed XML data. The process separated the discovery of unusual parser behavior from validation, in which the model attempted to create a working end-to-end exploit. Claude AI Finds SAML Flaws SAML is widely used for enterprise single sign-on , allowing an identity provider to send signed authentication assertions to a service provider. However, secure implementation depends on both components interpreting the same XML document in the same way. When signature verification and application logic process XML differently, attackers may be able to supply unsigned identity data that the application mistakenly trusts. The research identified full authentication bypasses in four projects, including Authentik, PHP litesaml/lightsaml, OneUptime, and Java saml-client. In three cases, the issue involved SAML signature wrapping , a long-standing attack class in which an attacker moves or injects XML elements so that a valid signature is verified on a different object. At the same time, the application reads identity information from another. The most notable issue affected Authentik, an open-source identity provider. Tracked as CVE-2026-57580, the flaw allowed an attacker to use an XML comment inside a SAML NameID value. Under certain non-default account-matching modes, Authentik could interpret the value before the comment as a victim’s username or email, even while the signed assertion remained valid. This could link an attacker-controlled external identity to the victim’s account, creating a persistent path to account takeover. Authentik fixed the vulnerability in versions 2026.2.6 and 2026.5.5. Organizations using inbound SAML sources with USERNAME_LINK or EMAIL_LINK matching should verify that they have applied the update. The vendor noted that default unique-identifier matching and outbound SAML provider deployments were not affected. The investigation also uncovered weaknesses outside standard SAML login responses. According to Oblique Security research , signature validation bypasses in authentication requests, attribute queries, and logout operations could enable information disclosure or arbitrary user logouts. Denial-of-service risks were also common. Several libraries accepted attacker-controlled XML documents that could trigger excessive memory usage during signature validation or XML transformation. Such weaknesses are especially dangerous because they can often be exploited before authentication. The findings reinforce a familiar message for identity teams: avoid custom SAML implementations whenever possible. Developers should use mature, actively maintained libraries, strictly validate signed elements, turn off dangerous XML transforms, impose document-size and resource limits, and test identity flows for parser differentials and signature wrapping attacks. AI can accelerate vulnerability discovery, but it can also expose how fragile legacy XML-based authentication implementations remain. Prevent incidents due to slow investigations. items.title: 451 Research report: How agentic AI is redefining identity security
items.summary: In the short time that AI agents have been a part of the enterprise, they have upended many of our bedrock assumptions about the nature of identity, access, development, and work itself. At 1Password, we’ve been in the trenches of the agentic revolution; we’ve seen its positive impact on productivity , and the serious concerns it raises about security . We’ve worked to build solutions that both harness AI’s potential and rein in its risks, and watched customers and colleagues grapple with the same issues. In order to better understand how the industry at large is facing the agentic moment, 1Password commissioned a Vanguard Report from 451 Research, titled A new access model for the agentic enterprise . The report describes how agentic AI is redefining access and identity, and lays out what C-level leaders can do to ensure a smooth transition to this new paradigm. Its core recommendations include: Start with discovery and visibility of AI agents and poorly governed non-human identities (NHIs). Move to just-in-time credential delivery , rather than static credentials and standing privileges. Implement guided remediation for developers so they can address NHI and agentic risk without interrupting their workflows. Ensure full auditability and clear attribution that ties every action to a specific human or agent identity and authorization context. Read on to explore the report’s findings, or download the full report here . An expanding identity perimeter, with agents already inside A new access model for the agentic enterprise begins by establishing that agentic AI is already deeply embedded in the enterprise. 69% of enterprises they surveyed have deployed AI agents, and 90% plan to do so within the next two years (these findings align with 1Password’s own research on agentic adoption). But while agents became ubiquitous almost overnight, the tools and strategies to secure them have not kept pace. This on its own isn’t unusual; the report reminds readers that this “pattern has repeated with every new technology advance of the past two decades.” Yet AI agents are unique in some crucial ways that set them apart from earlier revolutions in SaaS, cloud computing, and automation. “What makes agentic AI distinctly challenging to secure is not its scale but its unpredictability. Agents’ non-determinism breaks the core assumption of traditional access policy – that administrators can define in advance what a given identity should and should not do.” Adding to the complexity are developer workflows, which rely on NHIs like service accounts and API keys. In the short time that AI agents have been a part of the enterprise, they have upended many of our bedrock assumptions about the nature of identity, access, development, and work itself. At 1Password, we’ve been in the trenches of the agentic revolution; we’ve seen its positive impact on productivity, and the serious concerns it raises about security. We’ve worked to build solutions that both harness AI’s potential and rein in its risks, and watched customers and colleagues grapple with the same issues.

In order to better understand how the industry at large is facing the agentic moment, 1Password commissioned a Vanguard Report from 451 Research, titled A new access model for the agentic enterprise. The report describes how agentic AI is redefining access and identity, and lays out what C-level leaders can do to ensure a smooth transition to this new paradigm. Its core recommendations include:

  1. Start with discovery and visibility of AI agents and poorly governed non-human identities (NHIs).

  2. Move to just-in-time credential delivery, rather than static credentials and standing privileges.

  3. Implement guided remediation for developers so they can address NHI and agentic risk without interrupting their workflows.

  4. Ensure full auditability and clear attribution that ties every action to a specific human or agent identity and authorization context.

Read on to explore the report’s findings, or download the full report here.

An expanding identity perimeter, with agents already inside

A new access model for the agentic enterprise begins by establishing that agentic AI is already deeply embedded in the enterprise. 69% of enterprises they surveyed have deployed AI agents, and 90% plan to do so within the next two years (these findings align with 1Password’s own research on agentic adoption).

But while agents became ubiquitous almost overnight, the tools and strategies to secure them have not kept pace. This on its own isn’t unusual; the report reminds readers that this “pattern has repeated with every new technology advance of the past two decades.” Yet AI agents are unique in some crucial ways that set them apart from earlier revolutions in SaaS, cloud computing, and automation.

“What makes agentic AI distinctly challenging to secure is not its scale but its unpredictability. Agents’ non-determinism breaks the core assumption of traditional access policy – that administrators can define in advance what a given identity should and should not do.”

Adding to the complexity are developer workflows, which rely on NHIs like service accounts and API keys. These credentials are often poorly secured – 71% of developers use unsecure methods for handling NHIs – and they exist outside the visibility of IT and Security teams. Vulnerable and compromised NHIs have been a source of risk and friction for years, and that risk is multiplying as AI agents use them to take actions on the backend of corporate systems.

How to redefine access for the agentic enterprise

The next generation of access control has to work for humans, machines, and agents, while accommodating the non-determinism that sets agents apart. As the report explains, traditional IAM and PAM solutions are “structurally inadequate” for this world, and adjusting to it requires nothing less than a paradigm shift.

“The organizations that successfully navigate this transition will treat it as an architectural reset – rethinking identity security from the ground up to govern people, machines, and agents in a unified way, with a single control plane that integrates governance, policy management, and auditing.”

The report lays out a list of “fundamentals” that every organization must get right to meet the challenge of this moment. Among the non-negotiables are:

  • Visibility into every agent and credential in use, including plaintext secrets embedded in config files and on local disks.

  • A single system of record for credentials, “spanning human users, service accounts, machine identities, and AI agents.”

  • Grounding identity security in runtime authority, which means continuously evaluating an identity’s behavior against expected parameters and dynamically enforcing access barriers. (This is particularly crucial for agents, in order to contain the risks of non-determinism.)

Advice for leaders on the agentic security transition

451’s report closes with C-level guidance for managing this transformation on an organization level. It recommends getting cross-functional buy-in from every technical team, since they’re both using agents and responsible for securing them. Likewise, it advises that leaders work to enable developers, and to design governance policies and workflow integrations that “make secure agent provisioning the default, not an additional burden on top of delivery pressure.” This advice is aligned with 1Password’s longstanding commitment to “make the secure path the easy path.” Even in a security landscape undergoing such a profound transformation, that philosophy still holds true.
